name: Search with segment visibility

origin.note: Kranakis introduced segment visibility in a preprint of November 2026 [Kranakis2026Segment]; the earlier uses this note rests on are the author's own account.

summary: Robots search the plane for a point that they see when it lies on the segment joining two of them.
statement: $k \ge 2$ robots of unit speed start together at the origin $O$ of the plane, share a coordinate frame and a clock, and move deterministically. A stationary target lies at an unknown point $x \ne O$ at distance $d = \|x\| > 0$. The target is found at the first time $t$ at which $x$ lies on the closed segment joining the positions of two robots at time $t$; robots learn nothing about the target before. Depending on the setting the robots know $d$ or not; they never know the direction of $x$. **Time** is the competitive ratio: the supremum, over targets, of the time until the target is found divided by $d$.

primer.intro: Two or more lifeguards scan the sea for a buoy, and a buoy counts as seen as soon as it lies on the line of sight between two of them. Here $k \ge 2$ **robots**, points of unit speed, start together at the **origin** $O$ of the plane. A **target**, a point $x$ at distance $d$ from the origin, sits in an unknown direction. At every moment each pair of robots sees the straight **segment** that joins them, and the target is found the first time it lies on such a segment. The robots share a coordinate frame and a clock, and their routes are fixed in advance. The cost of a route plan is its **competitive ratio**: the largest value, over all targets, of the time until the target is found divided by $d$. In the basic version two robots do not know $d$.

ideas.title: Walk out in $k$ equally spaced directions
ideas.idea:
For $k \ge 3$ robots:
1. Number the robots $0, 1, \dots, k-1$.
2. Robot $i$ walks straight away from the origin in the direction at angle $2\pi i/k$, forever.
3. At time $t$ the robots are the corners of a regular $k$-gon of circumradius $t$; its sides are segments between neighbouring robots, and they sweep the plane as the polygon grows.
ideas.analysis: A target at distance $d$ whose direction is at angle $\varphi$ from the middle of its sector lies on a side of the polygon when $t\cos(\pi/k) = d\cos\varphi$, that is at time $d\cos\varphi/\cos(\pi/k)$. The worst targets are in the middle of a sector, so the competitive ratio is $1/\cos(\pi/k) = \sec(\pi/k)$: 2 for three robots, about 1.41 for four, and close to 1 for many robots. [Kranakis2026Segment] proves that no plan does better, whether or not the robots know $d$.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is optimal and needs no knowledge of $d$; the same walk is optimal for robots looking for a line.

ideas.title: Seeing a point is at least as hard as touching its tangent line
ideas.idea: Take a target $x$ at distance $d$ and the straight line through $x$ that is perpendicular to the direction of $x$ (the tangent at $x$ to the circle of radius $d$ about the origin). The robots start on the origin's side of that line. When $x$ lies on a segment between two robots, one of the two must be on the line or beyond it.
ideas.analysis: So a plan that finds every target point of the circle within time $Td$ also makes some robot touch every tangent line within time $Td$: it solves **shoreline search**, the search for a line at known distance. The best ratio for two robots that look for a line at known distance is $1+\sqrt3+\pi/6 \approx 3.256$ [Dobrev2020Shoreline], so no two-robot plan for points does better. [Kranakis2026Segment] gives a two-robot route that reaches exactly this ratio, so the bound is tight. When $d$ is unknown, the best known two-robot plan, two spirals on opposite sides of the origin, needs about $8.93$, and the best lower bound is about $3.29$.
ideas.why_it_matters: The reduction lets every lower bound for line search transfer to point search with segment visibility, which settles all cases except two robots that do not know $d$.

glossary.definition: a point that starts at the origin and moves at unit speed along a route fixed in advance; robots share a coordinate frame and a clock
the point $O$ of the plane where all robots start
a point $x \ne O$ at distance $d$ from the origin, in an unknown direction; it is found when it lies on a segment joining two robots
the straight piece joining the positions of two robots at the same time; the robots see every point on it
the largest value, over all targets, of the time until the target is found divided by $d$

history: Search for a target at an unknown place in the plane goes back to Bellman's question of how to find a line at known distance, and to the search for a line or a point by one or several robots of unit speed [BaezaYates1993Searching] [Dobrev2020Shoreline]. In those models a robot finds the target by touching it. Kranakis lets the robots see along the segments that join them, so a team sees a whole set of chords at each moment, and studies how much this helps; the answers are expressed through shoreline search, whose lower bounds carry over [Kranakis2026Segment].

measures.name: Competitive ratio
measures.description: worst-case time until the target lies on a segment between two robots, divided by its distance $d$ from the origin

axes.name: Number of robots

values.label: any number $k \ge 2$ of robots
values.definition: $k \ge 2$ robots; bounds are stated as functions of $k$.

values.label: two robots
values.definition: Two robots; the visible set at each time is the one segment between them.

axes.origin: Kranakis treats two robots separately because with two robots there is a single visible segment and the expanding-polygon algorithm does not exist; for $k \ge 3$ the optimum is $\sec(\pi/k)$ [Kranakis2026Segment]. The same split appears in shoreline search, where the cases $k = 2$ and $k = 3$ were the last to be settled for a known distance [Dobrev2020Shoreline].

axes.name: Knowledge of the distance

values.label: $d$ unknown
values.definition: The trajectories do not depend on $d$; the ratio is the supremum over all targets $x \ne O$ of $T(x)/\|x\|$.

values.label: $d$ known
values.definition: The robots know $d$ (not the direction of the target); the trajectories may depend on $d$, and the ratio is the supremum over targets with $\|x\| = d$ of $T(x)/d$.

axes.origin: Shoreline search was first studied at a known distance (Bellman's problem, solved for one searcher by Isbell, as reported by [Dobrev2020Shoreline]); Baeza-Yates, Culberson and Rawlins considered the unknown distance [BaezaYates1993Searching] (as reported by [Dobrev2020Shoreline]). Kranakis distinguishes the same two regimes for segment visibility and shows that for two robots not knowing $d$ costs at least $\sqrt{17}/4 - 1 \approx 0.031$ in the ratio, while for $k \ge 3$ it costs nothing [Kranakis2026Segment].

variants.title: Two robots, unknown distance
variants.summary: Two robots that do not know $d$ need a ratio between $\sqrt3+\pi/6+\sqrt{17}/4 \approx 3.2864$ and $\approx 8.9285$; the gap is open (a preprint).
variants.statement: Two robots; the trajectories do not depend on $d$, and every $d > 0$ is possible.

preconditions: targets on the three circles of radii $1/8$, $1/4$ and $1$ about the origin; holds even if the robots know these three radii
scale-invariant: also with circles of radii $1$, $2$, $8$, so it holds when $d \ge 1$ is promised
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 3.2 of [Kranakis2026Segment]. Below this ratio, the robot that first reaches the unit circle stays within distance $1/8$ of a line through the origin until then (Lemma 3.7), so the other robot alone must reach the levels $\pm1/8$, $\pm1/4$ on the perpendicular line, which forces ratio 4 (Lemma 3.4). It exceeds the known-distance optimum $1+\sqrt3+\pi/6$ by $\sqrt{17}/4 - 1 \approx 0.031$.

assumes: exact spirals from the origin, with infinitely many turns as $t \to 0$
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3.1): the robots follow two antipodal logarithmic spirals, so the visible segment is a diameter turning about the origin while it grows; ratio $e^{\pi\lambda}\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}/\lambda$, minimised at $\pi\lambda^*(1+\lambda^{*2}) = 1$, $\lambda^* \approx 0.2931$. Optimal only within this family of spirals.

time.note: $\approx 8.9285$ against $\approx 3.2864$: a constant gap, factor about 2.7.

open: Determine the optimal competitive ratio of two robots that do not know $d$: it lies between $\sqrt3+\pi/6+\sqrt{17}/4 \approx 3.2864$ and $\approx 8.9285$ [Kranakis2026Segment].

Do asymmetric, non-antipodal or non-spiral trajectories beat $\approx 8.9285$? The antipodal spirals see only along a diameter through the origin, while a segment between two moving robots can sweep chords that miss it [Kranakis2026Segment].
variants.notes: From the preprint [Kranakis2026Segment], read in full (arXiv v1). The known-distance optimum $1+\sqrt3+\pi/6$ is a lower bound here as well; the point of Theorem 3.2 is that the unknown distance costs strictly more. With a promised lower bound on $d$ the spiral needs a finite start, whose ratio the paper does not analyse. For comparison, two robots looking for a line (shoreline search) at unknown distance reach about $5.2644$ with two equally spaced logarithmic spirals (Baeza-Yates and Schott, as reported by [Dobrev2020Shoreline]); a line is touched no later than its tangency point is seen, so that bound does not carry over to segment search.

variants.title: Two robots, known distance
variants.summary: Two robots that know $d$ need exactly $1+\sqrt3+\pi/6 \approx 3.2556$, the same ratio as two robots looking for a line at known distance.
variants.statement: Two robots that know $d$ (not the direction of the target); the targets are the points of the circle of radius $d$ about the origin.

preconditions: targets on the circle of radius $d$, $d$ known
from shoreline search at known distance (Theorem 3 of [Dobrev2020Shoreline]): a robot touches the line tangent at the target no later than the target is seen

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2.1, Proposition 2.3): robot $\sigma \in \{\pm1\}$ walks straight to $(\sigma d/\sqrt3, d)$, along the tangent to $(\sigma\sqrt3 d/2, d/2)$, along the circle to $(\sigma d, 0)$, then straight down to $(\sigma d, -d)$; the last point found is $(0, -d)$.

variants.notes: From the preprint [Kranakis2026Segment], read in full (arXiv v1). The upper bound is proved directly; the lower bound is Theorem 3 of [Dobrev2020Shoreline] for shoreline search, transferred by the tangent-line reduction.

variants.title: $k \ge 3$ robots, unknown distance
variants.summary: With $k \ge 3$ robots the optimal ratio is exactly $\sec(\pi/k)$: the robots walk straight in $k$ equally spaced directions and the edges of the growing regular $k$-gon sweep the plane.
variants.statement: $k \ge 3$ robots that do not know $d$; every segment between two robots is visible (the algorithm uses only segments between neighbours on the $k$-gon). For $k = 2$ see the two-robot settings.

preconditions: holds even when every segment between two robots is visible
from shoreline search at unknown distance: Theorem 2.1 of [Acharjee2019Shoreline] for $k \ge 4$, Theorem 1 of [Dobrev2020Shoreline] for $k = 3$

assumes: only the $k$ segments between cyclic neighbours are monitored
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 4.1, Lemma 4.2): robot $i$ walks straight in direction $2\pi i/k$; a target at angle $\varphi$ from the bisector of its sector is found at time $d\cos\varphi/\cos(\pi/k)$, worst on the bisectors. Does not use $d$.

variants.notes: From the preprint [Kranakis2026Segment], read in full (arXiv v1). The ratio is the same as the optimum of shoreline search with $k \ge 3$ robots, whose upper bound $1/\cos(\pi/k)$ is the same walk along $k$ equally spaced rays (Baeza-Yates and Schott, as reported by [Dobrev2020Shoreline]): with three or more robots, seeing a point on a segment costs no more than touching its tangent line.

variants.title: $k \ge 3$ robots, known distance
variants.summary: Knowing $d$ does not help $k \ge 3$ robots: the optimal ratio is still exactly $\sec(\pi/k)$.
variants.statement: $k \ge 3$ robots that know $d$ (not the direction of the target); the targets are the points of the circle of radius $d$ about the origin.

preconditions: $k \ge 3$, targets on the circle of radius $d$, $d$ known
for $k \ge 4$ a direct argument: at any time $T < d/\cos(\pi/k)$ some open cone of angle $2\pi/k$ at the origin holds no robot, and no robot has touched the line tangent to the circle on its bisector
for $k = 3$ from Theorem 1 of [Dobrev2020Shoreline] (shoreline search at known distance, bound 2)
lower_bounds.note: Lemma 4.5 and Theorem 4.1 of [Kranakis2026Segment]; Lemma 4.5 adapts Section 2 of [Acharjee2019Shoreline] to a fixed distance.

results.note: The expanding $k$-gon of the unknown-distance setting; it does not use $d$ (Theorem 4.1).

variants.notes: From the preprint [Kranakis2026Segment], read in full (arXiv v1).
